title: Copper under the ocean, from an experimental spark to a redundant multinational grid, 1850-1900
register: documentary, wary of the single hero and the smooth plateau
summary: A private, state-assisted system for turning electrical impulses into hours saved: bank orders, ship intelligence, and government dispatches crossed in a day what a Cunard steamer needed ten to carry. It was built by promoters, naval hydrographers, manufacturers, and governments together, not by one man's idea, and it failed as often as it worked before 1866 made it durable. By 1900 it was no longer a single celebrated line but a pooled, competing, redundant grid run by British, French, American, and German companies at once.

nodes.name: Valentia Island, Foilhommerum Bay
nodes.note: The eastern landing of both the 1857-58 and the 1865-66 expeditions, and still the European anchor of the system in 1900. The permanent station building dates from 1868 and survives as part of a proposed transnational World Heritage ensemble with Heart's Content.

nodes.name: Trinity Bay, Bull Arm
nodes.note: The western landing of the first completed cable. Signals passed in August 1858 and the line was unusable by that September or October; the site was abandoned for Heart's Content when the durable cable came in 1866.

nodes.name: Heart's Content
nodes.note: Cable landed here 27 July 1866, giving the system its first durable terminus. The brick station begun in 1875 and finished in 1876 still stands with its equipment and cable shore section.

nodes.name: St John's
nodes.note: Gisborne's original telegraph hub, operating to Carbonear by March 1852 and by 1867 connected onward to Cape Ray, Heart's Content, and half a dozen other Newfoundland stations.

nodes.name: Cape Ray
nodes.note: Terminus of the overland Newfoundland line and the eastern end of the 1856 Cabot Strait cable, the last link that made the island a bridge rather than a destination.

nodes.name: Aspy Bay
nodes.note: Western landing of the 1856 Cabot Strait cable, joining Newfoundland's chain to the Nova Scotian and American telegraph networks a full two years before an ocean cable existed.

nodes.name: Halifax
nodes.note: A shipping, press, and telegraph hub on the onward route, never itself a landing of the deep-ocean cable but indispensable to reaching Boston and New York quickly.

nodes.name: London
nodes.note: The financial and governmental terminus. Messages reached it over ordinary British and Irish landlines rather than an uninterrupted ocean wire, but it was where the Atlantic Telegraph Company was organized in 1856 and where the subsidy was paid.

nodes.name: New York
nodes.note: The practical American commercial terminus for every generation of the system, from Cyrus Field's syndicate offices to the Commercial Cable Company's underground line ending on Wall Street in 1884.

nodes.name: Washington, D.C.
nodes.note: Recipient of Buchanan's reply to Victoria's 99-word message on 16 August 1858, and of government traffic given contractual priority under both British and French landing arrangements thereafter.

nodes.name: Brest, Déolen
nodes.note: French Atlantic landing complex, opened for the 1869 cable and expanded in 1879-80 for the Pouyer-Quertier route. Remains of the Déolen station survive.

nodes.name: Saint-Pierre
nodes.note: French relay island on the route from Brest, used again by the 1879 P-Q cable toward Cape Cod.

nodes.name: Duxbury, Cape Cod
nodes.note: Landing of the French-directed cables from Brest via Saint-Pierre. The surviving French Cable Station at Orleans belongs to the later, expanded complex.

nodes.name: Ballinskelligs
nodes.note: European end of the Direct United States Cable Company's route, built to compete with the Anglo-American combination and, after a price war, absorbed into its pool by 1877.

nodes.name: Tor Bay
nodes.note: Nova Scotian landing and relay of the Direct United States route, joining Ballinskelligs to Rye Beach.

nodes.name: Rye Beach
nodes.note: American landing of the Direct United States cable, built by Siemens and CS Faraday to break the Anglo-American combination's rates.

nodes.name: Waterville
nodes.note: Principal European station of the Commercial Cable Company, John Mackay and James Gordon Bennett Jr.'s challenge to the existing pool.

nodes.name: Canso, Dover Bay
nodes.note: Commercial Cable Company's Nova Scotian landing and relay hub, joining Waterville to the American stations.

nodes.name: Rockport
nodes.note: Commercial Cable station; a contemporary 1886 account names superintendent Robert Herne, an assistant, and six operators working there.

nodes.name: Coney Island, Far Rockaway
nodes.note: Commercial Cable's New York-area landing. An underground line ran a reported twenty-one miles through Brooklyn and across the East River Bridge to Wall Street, reducing dependence on rival landlines.

nodes.name: Horta, Fayal
nodes.note: Mid-Atlantic relay used by French, German, and Commercial systems in the 1890s, pivotal precisely because it was not owned by any single national system.

nodes.name: Emden, Borkum
nodes.note: German North Sea terminal complex of the Deutsche Atlantische Telegraphengesellschaft, opened for the Germany-Azores section on 26 May 1900, the dossier's chosen closing marker.

nodes.name: Porthcurno
nodes.note: Cornish landing connected to Brest and Déolen in 1880 to collect London traffic for the French system.

nodes.name: Weston-super-Mare
nodes.note: English feeder landing collecting traffic for the Commercial Cable Company from 1884-85.

nodes.name: Le Havre
nodes.note: French feeder landing for Commercial Cable Company traffic, 1884-85.

nodes.name: Paris
nodes.note: Financial and news-agency hub, home to Havas and to the corporate names behind the French Atlantic cables of 1869 and 1879.

nodes.name: Glass, Elliott and Company, East Greenwich
nodes.note: Cable manufacturer that produced core stock for the early Atlantic expeditions. Merged with the Gutta Percha Company in 1864 to form the Telegraph Construction and Maintenance Company.

nodes.name: Telegraph Construction and Maintenance Company works, Enderby Wharf
nodes.note: "Telcon," formed from the 1864 merger of Glass Elliott and the Gutta Percha Company, manufactured the durable 1865 and 1866 cables under contracts that by 1876 could require insulation resistance near 300 million ohms per nautical mile.

nodes.name: Siemens Brothers works, Woolwich
nodes.note: Built CS Faraday and the Direct United States cable, giving a second manufacturing house independent of the Telcon-Anglo-American combination.

nodes.name: Gutta-percha forests, Malay Archipelago
nodes.note: Source of the insulating gum without which no deep-sea cable was practicable. Harvesting usually felled the tree rather than tapping it, producing documented depletion; the precise tonnage used by any single Atlantic cable is not established.

nodes.name: The Atlantic Telegraph Company
nodes.note: Organized in London in October-November 1856 on a prospectus of £350,000, it laid the 1857-58 and 1865-66 cables before its interests were amalgamated with Anglo-American in 1873.

nodes.name: New York, Newfoundland and London Telegraph Company
nodes.note: Chartered 15 April 1854 with a fifty-year exclusive landing monopoly on Newfoundland; built the island's terrestrial chain before its interests passed into the 1873 Anglo-American amalgamation.

nodes.name: Anglo-American Telegraph Company
nodes.note: The financing vehicle for the 1866 expedition. It received £125,000 a year from Atlantic Telegraph Company revenues and £25,000 from the New York, Newfoundland and London Company under operating arrangements the Smithsonian's guide calls a 25 percent return.

nodes.name: French Atlantic Telegraph Company
nodes.note: Covers the Société du Câble Transatlantique Français, which opened the 1869 Brest-Saint-Pierre-Massachusetts route, and its 1879 successor the Compagnie française du télégraphe de Paris à New-York, presented as independent of British landing territory though later drawn into the pool.

nodes.name: Direct United States Cable Company
nodes.note: Built to undercut the Anglo-American combination via Rye Beach, Tor Bay, and Ballinskelligs. A price war and John Pender's acquisition of shares, contested in Pender v Lushington, ended with Direct inside the joint-purse pool by 1877.

nodes.name: Commercial Cable Company
nodes.note: John Mackay and James Gordon Bennett Jr.'s challenge to the pool, joining Waterville, Canso, and Rockport to Mackay's Postal Telegraph system and lowering rates again by entering independent of the existing companies.

nodes.name: Deutsche Atlantische Telegraphengesellschaft
nodes.note: Organized by Felten and Guilleaume in 1899; opened Germany-Azores on 26 May 1900 and the full Germany-Azores-New York line on 28 August 1900, the strategic diversification that closes this dossier's period.

nodes.name: The joint-purse pool
nodes.note: Not a company but a recurring arrangement: a challenger enters, rates fall to a shilling a word, the challenger's cable fails or its finances weaken, and an alliance restores the rate to two shillings. A U.S. congressional report described the pattern as a documented sequence, not an allegation.

nodes.name: British Government
nodes.note: Committed naval surveying, ships, and an annual subsidy of £14,000, reducible to £10,000, for a stated twenty-five-year period, in exchange for priority on government messages.

nodes.name: United States Government
nodes.note: Supplied USS Niagara and naval assistance to the 1857-58 expedition, exchanged the Victoria-Buchanan messages of 1858, and in 1898 cut and censored cables serving Cuba and the Philippines.

nodes.name: Newfoundland Government
nodes.note: Enacted the 15 April 1854 charter granting a fifty-year exclusive landing monopoly, retained a pre-emption right after twenty years, and declined to exercise it in 1874 despite newspaper attacks on the concession's rates.

nodes.name: USS Niagara
nodes.note: One of the two naval vessels, alongside HMS Agamemnon, that spliced and laid the 1858 cable, meeting mid-ocean and steaming in opposite directions.

nodes.name: HMS Agamemnon
nodes.note: British naval vessel supplied for the 1857-58 expedition, Niagara's counterpart in laying and completing the first Atlantic cable.

nodes.name: Great Eastern
nodes.note: The one ship large enough to carry an entire Atlantic cable. Laid the durable 1866 line, then recovered and completed the lost 1865 cable, and continued laying and repair work into the 1870s.

nodes.name: CS Faraday
nodes.note: Purpose-built for Siemens, laid the Direct United States cable and, over its career, an estimated 50,000 nautical miles of cable by the compiled vessel record.

nodes.name: CS Mackay-Bennett
nodes.note: Roughly 2,000-gross-ton repair vessel launched in 1884 for the Commercial Cable Company, with cable machinery, electric lighting, and a specialized electrical staff.

nodes.name: Cyrus W. Field
nodes.note: Coordinated American finance, British investment, government support, and repeated expeditions after Gisborne approached him in 1854. His central promotional role runs through the 1873 amalgamation; the claim that he alone conceived the cable is a biographical simplification.

nodes.name: John Pender
nodes.note: Became the dominant British cable financier through holdings, mergers, and joint-purse arrangements, acquiring Direct United States shares in a fight litigated as Pender v Lushington. Critics called him the Cable King.

nodes.name: William Thomson, Lord Kelvin
nodes.note: Analyzed signal retardation in long cables, developed the sensitive mirror galvanometer and later the siphon recorder, and advised on paying-out forces across successive expeditions.

nodes.name: Edward Orange Wildman Whitehouse
nodes.note: The Atlantic Telegraph Company's electrician in 1858, who favored high-voltage induction coils against Thomson's low-voltage sensitivity. The 1861 Joint Committee found manufacture, testing, and handling also culpable rather than blaming him alone.

nodes.name: John William Mackay
nodes.note: Used mining wealth to finance the Commercial Cable Company's challenge to the established pool.

nodes.name: James Gordon Bennett Jr.
nodes.note: Proprietor of the New York Herald, whose commercial interest in cheaper news transmission and strategic interest in an independent line helped fund the Commercial Cable Company alongside Mackay.

edges.note: The predecessor system the cable displaced: Cunard steamers carried news across in about ten days under favorable conditions.
The 1857-58 expedition's cable, carrying several hundred messages before the line failed that autumn.
The durable 1866 cable, laid by Great Eastern in a fourteen-day crossing beginning 13 July, plus the recovered and completed 1865 line spliced in that September.
The 1856 Cabot Strait cable, replacing an 1855 attempt lost from the barque Sarah L. Bryant.
Newfoundland's difficult overland line, cleared and maintained through sparsely settled country.
Irish and British landline connection; the Atlantic cable was never operationally only its ocean segment.
Opened 1869, presented as an alternative less dependent on British landing territory.
1880 connection built to collect London traffic for the P-Q company's renewed route.
The Direct United States route, 1874-75.
Commercial Cable Company's Atlantic crossing, opened 1884.
The company's own underground line, run through Brooklyn and across the East River Bridge to Wall Street to avoid dependence on rival landlines.
Opened 26 May 1900.
Completed the German system on 28 August 1900, the dossier's closing marker.
